title: Characterization of Protein Precipitation Methods of Clinical Samples for Simple and Low-Cost Methods to Enhance the Depth and Breadth of Plasma Proteomics
projectDescription: Plasma is an abundant source of proteins and potential biomarkers to aid in the detection, diagnosis, and prognosis of human diseases.  These proteins are often present at low levels in the blood and difficult to identify and measure due to the large dynamic range.  Abundant protein precipitation with perchloric acid (PerCA) can increase protein identifications and depth of plasma proteomic studies.  The goal of this work was to characterize and compare various protein precipitation methods related to plasma proteomic depth and breadth.  Three acid- and four solvent-based precipitation methods were evaluated.  All methods tested provided excellent plasma proteomic coverage (>600 identified protein groups) and detected protein in the low pg/ml range.  Functional enrichment analysis revealed subtle differences within and larger changes between the precipitant groups.  Methanol-based precipitation outperformed the other methods based on identifications and reproducibility.  The methods’ performance was verified using eight lung cancer patient samples, where >700 protein groups were measured and proteins with an estimated plasma concentration of ~10 pg/ml were detected.  Various protein precipitation agents are amenable to extending the depth and breadth of plasma proteomes.  These data can guide investigators to implement inexpensive, high-throughput methods for their plasma proteomic workflows.
sampleProcessingProtocol: 2.1 Plasma Samples  Plasma samples used in the study were derived from a commercial pool of human plasma collected in K2EDTA tubes (Innovative Research) or from consented lung cancer patients treated at the Penn State Cancer Institute on an IRB-approved protocol (STUDY00000998) collected in K2EDTA tubes.  Plasma was obtained from the patient’s blood by centrifugation at 1500xg for 15 min.  The upper plasma layer was removed and centrifuged at 5,000xg for 10 min, and the resulting supernatant was aliquoted into freezer tubes and stored at -80oC. 2.2 Acid Precipitation Sample Preparation Acid precipitation was performed in a 96-well format, similar to that described by Viode et al. 2023 (Viode et al., 2023).  Fifty microliters of plasma were diluted in water and then the acid was added to achieve the appropriate final concentration of precipitant in 500 µl.  After mixing, the samples were allowed to equilibrate at -20oC for 15 min before centrifugation at 4oC and 3,200xg for 20 min.  Four hundred microliters of the supernatant were mixed with 40 µl of 1% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), except for TFA-treated samples, and the sample was loaded onto a conditioned Oasis Prime HLB µElute plate (Waters).  Conditioning included one wash each with methanol and 90% acetonitrile (ACN) plus 0.1% TFA, then equilibrated with two washed with 0.1% TFA in water.  Wells were washed twice after loading with 0.1% TFA in water and proteins were eluted in 90% ACN with 0.1% TFA before drying a speedvac at 45oC.  Proteins were suspended in 35 µl of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate (ABC) by sonication for 5 min before the addition of 0.5 µg Trypsin (Promega).  Digestion progressed overnight at 37oC and was stopped by the addition of 5 µl of 10% formic acid (FA).  Sample protein concentrations at A280 were checked with a NanoDrop OneC spectrometer and diluted to ~300 ng/µl with LC loading buffer (0.1% FA).  Samples were stored at -80oC until LC-MS analysis. 2.3 Organic Solvent Precipitation Sample Preparation  Samples were prepared in a 96-well format.  Fifty microliters of plasma were diluted in water then the solvent was added to achieve the appropriate final concentration of precipitant in 500 µl.  After mixing, the samples were allowed to equilibrate at -20oC for 15 min before centrifugation at 4oC and 3,200xg for 20 min.  Four hundred microliters of the supernatant were dried in a speedvac at 45oC for 70 min.  The remaining liquid was mixed with 600 ul of 0.2% TFA and the entire contents were loaded onto a conditioned Oasis Prime HLB µElute plate (Waters).  Wells were washed twice after loading with 0.1% TFA in water and proteins were eluted in 90% ACN with 0.1% TFA before drying a speedvac at 45oC.  Proteins were suspended in 35 µl of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate (ABC) by sonication for 5 min before the addition of 0.5 µg Trypsin (Promega).  Digestion progressed overnight at 37oC and was stopped by the addition of 5 µl of 10% formic acid (FA).  Sample protein concentrations at A280 were checked with a NanoDrop spectrometer and diluted to ~300 ng/µl with LC loading buffer (0.1% FA).  Samples were stored at -80oC until LC-MS analysis. 2.4 LC-MS Acquisition  Samples were processed in a single batch for each of the experiments.  The samples were run in a single batch for the initial experiment and then in three batches for the final experiment.  Instrument performance at the precursor and protein levels was monitored throughout the LC-MS runs with a commercially digested Yeast peptide sample (Promega) measured after every 10 (Fig. S1) or 8 (Fig. S2) runs.  The run order was randomized for each replicate group using the random number generator in Excel (Microsoft). One microliter of each sample (~300 ng) was analyzed using a NanoElute LC connected to a timsTOF Flex (Bruker) mass spectrometer.  The NamoElute used a 50-sample-per-day method with a ~20 min gradient from 2%-35% B (acetonitrile with 0.1% formic acid) and an ~28 min cycle time.  The sample was loaded onto a µ-Precolumn with PepMap C18 (5x0.3 mm, Thermo Scientific) trap and then separated with a 150 x 0.15 mm C18 PepSep column (Bruker). The mass spectrometer was operated in either DDA- or diaPASEF modes.  DDA-PASEF mode included four PASEF scans per cycle and the following parameters; m/z range 100-1700, mobility range 0.7-1.45 V.s/cm2, accumulation and ramp time was set to 100 ms, and target intensity was set to 5000.  For diaPASEF, the m/z range was 100-1700, the mobility range was 0.57-1.65 the ramp and accumulation times were set to 100 ms.  Twenty-four variable DIA isolation windows across 12 ion-mobility scans per cycle were optimized to fit the expected precursor ion cloud from our in-silico peptide library using the pydiAID tool (Table S1) (Skowronek et al., 2022).  The method had a total cycle time of ~1.38 s.
dataProcessingProtocol: 2.5 Data Searches  DDA data was searched against a UniProt human canonical protein database (IP000005640_9606; ~20,000 proteins) with decoys and contaminants added, using the FragPipe pipeline that included MSFragger, Percolator, and IonQuant (Kong et al., 2017; Teo et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2020).  Default settings were used for the search and C-carbamidomethylation was removed as a modification.  Data was filtered at the precursor and protein levels for a 1% FDR.   DIA data was searched using DIA-NN (v.1.8.0 and 1.8.2 beta 22) against an in-silico library generated by DIA-NN  from a list of plasma peptides found in the Human Plasma Peptide Atlas (EW et al., 2021), as reported previously (Rice & Belani, 2022).  Searches were conducted with default settings except without C-carbamidomethylation modifications, the match-between-runs function was activated, and the composite (high-precision) quantitation strategy was selected.  Search results were filtered for a 1% FDR at the precursor and protein levels.  The mass spectrometry proteomics data and search results have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifiers; PXD050216, , and , Fig. 1 DDA, Fig. 1 DIA, and Fig. 4 DIA data, respectively.
